questions.a: Grouping by common properties makes study and choice of materials easy and systematic.

questions.q: On what properties can materials be grouped?
questions.a: Appearance (lustre), hardness, solubility, floating, transparency - and metal or non-metal.

questions.q: Give one object that can be made of many materials.
questions.a: A chair - wood, plastic, metal or cane can all make chairs.
The shine of a material - metals like iron, copper and gold show it when fresh.

questions.q: Why do old iron articles lose their shine?
questions.a: A dull layer of rust covers the metal, hiding its natural lustre.
Gold and copper (freshly cut metals shine).

questions.q: What is hardness of a material?
questions.a: Its resistance to scratches and dents - hard materials scratch soft ones.

questions.q: Name the softest and a very hard material you know.
questions.a: Soft: chalk. Hard: iron nail (diamond is hardest in nature).

questions.q: Can a hard material be scratched by a soft one?
questions.a: No - only a harder material can scratch a softer one.
The ability of a substance to dissolve in a liquid (usually water) to form a transparent solution.

questions.q: Name two soluble and two insoluble substances in water.
questions.a: Soluble: sugar, salt. Insoluble: sand, chalk powder.

questions.q: How do we know a substance has dissolved completely?
questions.a: The water turns clear (not cloudy) and no particles settle at the bottom.

questions.q: On what does floating or sinking of an object depend?
questions.a: On its weight (density) compared with water - lighter things float, heavier sink.

questions.q: Name two materials that float and two that sink in water.
questions.a: Float: wood, cork, oil. Sink: iron nail, stone.

questions.q: Why does a heavy wooden log float but a small iron nail sinks?
questions.a: Wood is less dense than water; iron is denser, whatever the size.

questions.q: Group materials as transparent, translucent and opaque with examples.
questions.a: Transparent: glass, clear water. Translucent: butter paper, frosted glass. Opaque: wood, metal sheet.

questions.q: Through which material can we see objects clearly?
questions.a: Transparent materials - they let nearly all light pass straight through.

questions.q: Why are windows made of glass and doors of wood?
questions.a: Glass is transparent to let light in; wood is opaque for privacy and strength.
